rv.q: This multifaceted and personal homage to – and collaboration with – composer Philip Glass is a transcendent tapestry suffused with joy and wonder.
What’s certain is that this homage to the creative spirit is an absolute one-off, and a vividly theatrical one.
Far from naff or dull, this is in fact a cheeky show, and a fun show, and a deeply profound show.

The show can feel whimsical and even self-indulgent, and it's definitely too long. But gradually you realise that the whole piece is working... to build a fragile, meditative piece of theatre that is buzzingly immediate.
Director, writer and actor Phelim McDermott’s musing on creativity and his relationship with composer Philip Glass and his music strikes me as quite beautiful, but some will find it exasperating.

Given that McDermott is a devotee not only of Glass but of the Japanese art of kintsugi – the mending of broken pottery with a gold-based glue – this second artistic flowering of a scuppered project is the perfect outcome.
Go see this extraordinary production to find out for yourself how that leger de main works.
When the spell is broken, we emerge refreshed and hopeful while a tug of the inevitable whispers in the undertow of sound waves.
Dense, profound, a lecture with stage play and comedy to help it go down, Tao of Glass is a delight, but you must stay alert.
Tao of Glass is many things; delightfully funny, visually impressive, challengingly erudite and exquisitely beautiful.
Fortunately, for the most part, it also happens to be bloody marvellous.
Thoughtful, visually striking and emotionally resonant, Tao of Glass invites audiences to slow down, listen and reflect.
It’s fantastical and disarming in a way that normally seems out of reach for adult theatre.
Otherwise, the art of storytelling blossoms in this curious and fascinating show.
But the whole play feels like it could be cut by at least an hour.
The contemplation and deep thought that Tao of Glass inspires is truly unique, unlike anything else I've experienced before in a theatre.
It feels close to miraculous that a piece this experimental, this gentle and this patient can exist on a West End stage.
Tao of Glass is a show like no other and one that deserves to be seen to be believed.

However, only gradually does one become aware that it is also profoundly philosophical. In talking to the audience, McDermott weaves together his burgeoning career in the theatre with his growing passion for Glass’s music.
Tao of Glass is original, imaginary and deeply moving.

Consistently less than the sum of its intriguing parts, this is a frustrating experience and perhaps ultimately an illustration of how and why it is not a good idea for the writer and lead performer also to be the main director of the production.
Tao of Glass is easy to recommend. It's a unique piece which defies classification or expectation, and is an easy success on all fronts.
But, at nearly three hours, it feels somewhat indulgent, and the musical elements are subsumed by the storytelling.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace McDermott's playful, profound meditation on Philip Glass and creativity, praising its beauty and theatrical magic, though some find the pacing uneven and the introspection occasionally self-indulgent.
